title: Louisville: Where the Kentucky Derby Runs and Muhammad Ali Danced
summary: Kentucky's largest city where Churchill Downs has hosted the most exciting two minutes in sports since 1875, where Muhammad Ali learned to float like a butterfly, where bourbon flows freely along Whiskey Row, and where the Louisville Slugger has been swinging since 1884.

content.intro: On the first Saturday of every May, 150,000 people crowd into Churchill Downs to watch three-year-old thoroughbreds run a mile and a quarter while wearing elaborate hats and drinking mint juleps. The Kentucky Derby has been Louisville's defining moment since 1875, but this city on the Ohio River has been defining American culture in other ways too. Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay here in 1942, learned to box at a local gym, and transformed himself into the greatest - his funeral in 2016 stopped traffic across the city as mourners lined the streets. The Louisville Slugger bat company has been hand-crafting baseball's most famous weapon since 1884; the world's largest bat stands outside their factory, 120 feet of steel and sculpture. Old Louisville contains the largest Victorian preservation district in America, block after block of ornate mansions built by bourbon and tobacco money. The bourbon itself flows along Whiskey Row downtown, where distilleries that once served the entire nation are reviving after a century of dormancy. Louisville sits at the Falls of the Ohio, where the river drops 26 feet and forced early travelers to portage - the Gateway to the South, the city calls itself, though it feels like the gateway to everywhere.

sections.title: The Kentucky Derby
sections.body: Churchill Downs opened in 1875, and the Kentucky Derby has run every year since - through wars, depressions, and pandemics. The twin spires of the grandstand, added in 1895, are the most recognizable symbol in horse racing. The race itself takes about two minutes, but Derby Day is a festival: the infield packed with 80,000 revelers who can barely see the track, the grandstands filled with women in extravagant hats and men in seersucker suits, everyone drinking mint juleps made from bourbon, sugar, and fresh mint. The Kentucky Derby Festival runs for two weeks before the race - Thunder Over Louisville launches it with the largest annual fireworks display in North America. The Derby winner is draped in a blanket of 554 roses, the Run for the Roses complete. The Kentucky Derby Museum preserves the history; the track hosts racing from April to November. But Derby Day itself is sacrament, the moment when Louisville becomes the center of the sporting world.

sections.title: Muhammad Ali's Louisville
sections.body: Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. was born in Louisville on January 17, 1942, in a pink house on Grand Avenue. At twelve, after his bicycle was stolen, he found Joe Martin's boxing gym and began the transformation that would make him the greatest heavyweight champion in history. He won Olympic gold in Rome in 1960, turned professional, and defeated Sonny Liston in 1964, the same year he joined the Nation of Islam and became Muhammad Ali. His refusal to be drafted for Vietnam cost him his title and three years of his career, but he returned to win the championship two more times. Ali died in Phoenix in 2016, but Louisville claimed him home - his funeral procession wound through the streets where he had grown up, past the house on Grand Avenue, past the gym where he had learned to dance and punch. The Muhammad Ali Center downtown preserves his legacy, not just as a boxer but as an activist, humanitarian, and Louisville's most famous son.

sections.title: Bourbon and Baseball
sections.body: The Louisville Slugger has been the official bat of Major League Baseball since 1884, when Bud Hillerich turned a bat on his father's lathe for Pete Browning of the Louisville Eclipse. The factory on Main Street still produces 1.8 million bats annually; the world's largest bat, 120 feet tall and weighing 68,000 pounds, leans against the building. Visitors can tour the factory and receive a miniature souvenir bat. A few blocks away, Whiskey Row preserves the distilleries that once made Louisville the bourbon capital of America. Prohibition destroyed the industry - Kentucky had 200 distilleries before 1920, six after 1933 - but the bourbon renaissance has returned. The Evan Williams Bourbon Experience, Angel's Envy, and Michter's Fort Nelson offer tours and tastings along Main Street. The Urban Bourbon Trail connects over 40 bars and restaurants serving Kentucky's signature spirit. Louisville made America's bat and America's whiskey; both are still being made.

sections.title: Victorian Splendor
sections.body: Old Louisville is the largest Victorian preservation district in the United States, 48 square blocks of mansions built between 1880 and 1910 by families who made fortunes in bourbon, tobacco, and river trade. The neighborhood nearly died in the mid-twentieth century - mansions were subdivided into apartments, demolished for parking lots, abandoned to decay. Preservationists saved it beginning in the 1970s, and today Old Louisville feels like stepping into the Gilded Age. St. James Court, built around a fountain imported from the 1893 World's Fair, hosts the St. James Court Art Show every October - half a million visitors browse art among the Victorian facades. The Speed Art Museum, adjacent to Old Louisville on the University of Louisville campus, houses Kentucky's largest art collection in a building that melds 1920s Beaux-Arts with contemporary addition. The ornate architecture reminds visitors that Louisville was once one of America's wealthiest cities.

sections.title: River City Geography
sections.body: Louisville International Airport (SDF) serves as UPS's worldwide hub - the world's largest automated package handling facility processes millions of packages nightly, visible from the air as a hive of activity. I-64 runs east-west through the city; I-65 runs north-south, crossing the Ohio River into Indiana on bridges that connect Louisville to its northern suburbs. The Ohio River defines the city's northern border, the Falls of the Ohio creating the rapids that forced early settlers to stop here. Big Four Bridge, a former railroad crossing, now carries pedestrians and cyclists between Louisville's Waterfront Park and Jeffersonville, Indiana. From altitude, Louisville appears along the river bend where the falls once blocked navigation - the downtown skyline modest but distinctive, Churchill Downs visible to the south with its iconic twin spires, the UPS hub sprawling near the airport. What appears from the air as Kentucky's largest city is where the Derby runs, where Ali danced, where bourbon flows, and where the Louisville Slugger still cracks against fastballs.

content.flightContext: Located at 38.25°N, 85.77°W on the south bank of the Ohio River at the Falls of the Ohio in north-central Kentucky. From altitude, Louisville appears at the river's bend - Churchill Downs' twin spires visible to the south, the UPS Worldport hub sprawling near the airport, the Ohio River bridges crossing to Indiana. What appears from the air as Kentucky's largest city is where the Kentucky Derby has run since 1875 and where Muhammad Ali learned to box.
